Project Title: Project 150
Executive Summary: Project 150 will empower One Hundred and Fifty (150) women and youths in organic poultry farming, the farmers will be trained and provided with farm inputs (chicks, medications & feed)  and access to market their harvested produce (table-size broilers) through an off-taker partnership with our enterprise.
Innovation Description: The problems: 1) Post-harvest losses due to inaccessible market: lack of accessible market often leads to significant losses in terms of high feed consumption cost and higher chances of mortality which impact the income of farmers negatively. 2) Limited access to farm inputs: the high cost of farm inputs has made it inaccessible for farmers , most small-holder farmers have either shut-down or are operating below production capacity. This has invariably affected the supply of poultry products in my community. 3) Antibiotic resistance: antibiotic resistance in poultry production is a growing treat that is being given little or no attention. Some researches have shown that the abuse of antibiotic drugs in livestock affects both animals and humans and creates mutants (new microbes) that are resistant to antibiotics. There is an urgent need to address the growing trend. Solution: Our business model is designed to provide the following solutions to tackle the above mentioned problems:  1) Provide access to market: at harvest, our enterprise will off-take the harvested broilers at prevailing market price, process and market the finished products through our distribution channels.  2) Input distribution: farm inputs (chicks, medication & feed) will be distributed to small-holder farmers and the farmer repays for the inputs with harvested produce at 0% interest.  3)Provide alternative medicines: herbal medicines that are safe for both animal and human consumption will be provided to farmers as replacement for antibiotic drugs. The farmers will be trained on the use and benefits of herbal medicines.

Project Title: Transforming Food Access: Empowering Healthier Choices in Underserved Communities
Executive Summary: Saba Grocers Initiative coordinates a Collective Purchasing Agreement (CPA) which created fresh produce access in  food deserts  by distributing low-volume orders of fruits and vegetables to Oakland corner stores at wholesale prices. Prior to our project, these stores carried only tobacco, alcohol and junk foods. By sourcing from BIPOC farmers and coordinating economies of scale in underserved communities, we increase healthy food availability,  mitigate supply chain inequities and support small businesses and underserved communities.
Innovation Description: The ease with which corner stores can acquire alcohol and tobacco through supply chain networks with free distribution, stocking, and marketing creates an environment where unhealthy products outcompete healthy ones. In response to this, we developed a Collective Purchasing Agreement (CPA) - a structural investment in the local food system - to build equity for store owners wishing to provide healthy produce. Our CPA increases fresh food access and affordability in food apartheid neighborhoods. Saba is the only produce delivery service available to corner stores in Oakland, meeting challenges posed by Social Determinants of Health (SDoH) in our neighborhoods. Since initiation we have distributed over $670,000 worth of produce to stores that carried only junk food and beverages prior to our service.  The City of Oakland predicts half of African-American and Latinx children will develop diabetes in their lifetime along with other diet related diseases. Our recent survey indicated that: 75% of corner store clientele identified as Black or African American, 58% are caregivers of children, and 63%  strongly disagreed  with the statement  It s easy for me to find affordable, quality fresh produce where I live.  Since 2020, we have made 2,600+ deliveries, distributing produce to 14 corner stores in 14 neighborhoods with a consistent and diverse supply of fresh produce, including culturally relevant items. We are changing the conditions, so that small businesses and residents can circumvent barriers to accessing produce, and reclaiming the social narrative alongside the shelf space now available for fruits and vegetables.

Project Title: Black Soldier Fly farming: Changing trash to cash
Executive Summary: The project, driven by a circular economy model, addresses Kenya's escalating organic solid waste crisis, with 60-70% of waste being organic countrywide and 51% as biowaste in Kasarani subcounty, Nairobi. Rearing black soldier fly colonies in specialized screen houses, the initiative aims to produce protein-rich feeds for fish, poultry, and pigs while reducing waste pollution. This becomes crucial in the face of rapid urbanization and population growth, which have led to significant waste generation, especially in major cities like Nairobi. The project not only eliminates open dumping but also addresses health concerns linked to unmanaged waste. It generates employment for the youth, contributing to livelihood transformation, and mitigates climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions associated with severe climate effects like storms and droughts. Additionally, it provides protein-rich animal feeds, addressing food security challenges. The project's beneficiaries include urban farmers, unemployed youth, community-based organizations, and youth groups. With statistics highlighting the extent of waste issues, the initiative serves as a learning site for bio-waste processing, waste segregation, and environmental protection, fostering positive impacts on both the community and the environment.

Project Title: Black Soldier Fly Farming: Trash to Cash
Executive Summary: The project uses Black Soldier Fly (BSF) to transform organic waste into organic fertilizer (frass) and high-protein animal feed to boost food sustainability and security for smallholder farmers. By producing affordable, nutrient-rich livestock feed and climate-smart fertilizer, the project enhances crop yields, reduces environmental impact, and creates economic opportunities. It further promotes circular economies, empowers farmers with training, and strengthens local food systems, contributing to healthier communities and resilient agricultural practices.
Innovation Description: The Black Soldier Fly (BSF) project addresses two significant challenges in Nairobi: the high cost of animal feed for farmers and the management of organic waste. In Kenya, feeding costs constitute 60 80% of total production expenses for most farmers, straining smallholder farmers' profitability. In Nairobi, where the project is based, the city generates approximately 2,400 tonnes of waste daily, with over 50% being organic, leading to environmental concerns.  The BSF project offers an innovative solution by utilizing BSF larvae to convert organic waste into high-protein animal feed and organic fertilizer, the frass (in the ratio of 5:1 (5 kgs of biowaste produces 1 kg of frass). They further convert the nutrients of the wastes into 42% protein and 35% feedstuff through bioconversion process. This bioconversion process reduces waste in landfills and provides farmers with affordable, nutritious feed alternatives, the BSF larvae, thereby lowering production costs and enhancing livestock productivity. Additionally, the frass serves as a nutrient-rich fertilizer, promoting sustainable crop production and reducing reliance on chemical fertilizers. Scientific insights into the BSF's efficient waste conversion capabilities (bioconversion) and high protein content have led to this sustainable approach. The immediate benefits include cost savings for farmers, improved animal health due to better nutrition, and enhanced crop yields from organic fertilization. Sustainably, the project contributes to environmental conservation by managing organic waste and supports economic empowerment within local communities through job creation and improved agricultural productivity.

Project Title: Building Capacity For a Safe and Transparent Dairy Supply Chain in the Rwandan Eastern Province
Executive Summary: This project focuses on distributing the Safi device to 60 dairy farmers in Rwanda s Eastern Province. Complementary to the device are educational efforts that will teach farmers and their communities about the importance of selling/consuming pasteurized milk. If successful, this pilot will open up the opportunity for Safi to work with the Rwandan National Dairy Platform, Heifer International and Ripple Effect Rwanda, and the 15,000 dairy farmers in their networks.
Innovation Description: East Africa has the highest global incidence of milk-borne disease. Alarmingly, 30% of deaths in children under 5. This is due to a lack of access to safe and quality milk, with up to 90% of milk in East Africa being sold raw by small scale milk sellers in the unregulated, informal market. The challenges of the current dairy supply chain are burdened by many factors but most importantly the lack of adequate traceability and tools to ensure safety.   At Safi, we have patented the world's first, small-scale pasteurization control unit targeted towards small-scale dairy farmers and vendors. The device kills milk-borne diseases all while retaining the key nutrients of milk. It is affordable, powered by renewable energy sources, and allows farmers to easily pasteurize their differentiating daily yields.   To address inadequate traceability, at the core of the product is a digital tracking system that remotely records milk pasteurization data and centralizes production information for regulators and governments.   The Safi solution ensures that the ability to pasteurize milk is democratized to smallholder farmers who supply up to 90% of milk sold in these markets. This allows farmers to earn more money per litre of milk, and also makes pasteurized milk more accessible and affordable to the general public. Safi is also looking to collaborate with the  One Cup, One Child  school feeding program in Rwanda to get a cup of safe milk to every school child in Rwanda. Therefore, Safi provides clear benefits to farmers, consumers and their communities.

Project Title: Ending malnutrition for 100 million people by guaranteeing that every meal, for every mother and child, contains lifesaving nutrients forever.
Executive Summary: Full bellies aren't enough; everyone needs essential nutrients to develop and maintain good health. Yet, 8,000 kids die every day due to micronutrient deficiencies. Sanku is solving this by partnering with local millers who produce and sell the staple foods families consume daily, empowering them to sustainably fortify flour. Sanku installs the Dosifier an award-winning IoT-enabled technology that attaches to local mills and adds a precise amount of critical nutrients into each bag of flour.
Innovation Description: Micronutrient deficiency, also known as hidden hunger, affects one in five Africans, particularly in low-income regions, where diets often comprise calorie-dense but nutrient-poor staples such as maize and wheat flour, leading to devastating but preventable health issues including intellectual disabilities in children, weakened immune systems, increased maternal mortality, as well as reduced economic productivity. With over 280 million undernourished people in Africa 57 million more since the COVID-19 pandemic micronutrient deficiency is an escalating public health crisis.    Food fortification is one of the most effective, safe, and cost-efficient interventions for addressing malnutrition, with nearly a century of proven success. A 2020 review of 50 studies found that fortifying staple foods like maize and wheat flour reduced anemia rates by 34%, neural tube defects by 41%, and vitamin A deficiency for three million children in one year, significantly lowering mortality. However, typical initiatives in Africa often fail to reach the most vulnerable populations and rural poor, who lack access to centrally processed foods.    Sanku exists to fulfil this critical need by partnering with and empowering small and medium-scale millers to sustainably fortify flour for the hardest-to-reach places in Eastern Africa. These millers produce and sell staple foods that families consume daily. Sanku installs  a dosifier, an award-winning IoT-enabled technology that attaches to local mills and adds a precise amount of critical nutrients into each bag of flour. This ensures that every bag of flour produced contains the necessary vitamins and minerals to support healthy growth and development.

Project Title: Khumba
Executive Summary: Khumba ransforms crop residue into dual-impact products: nutritious mushrooms for human consumption and mycorrhizal-enriched soil amendments. By leveraging our existing infrastructure in Punjab and proprietary fermentation processes, we convert agricultural waste that would otherwise be burned into high-value food products while simultaneously developing soil-enhancing biologicals. This circular solution addresses food security, farmer income, soil health, and air pollution challenges in one integrated system.
Innovation Description: India faces a critical agricultural challenge: over 20 million tons of rice straw are burned annually in Punjab and Haryana, creating severe air pollution and destroying valuable biomass. Simultaneously, the region struggles with degrading soil health and the need for sustainable protein sources. Our innovation addresses these interconnected challenges through a novel bioconversion approach.  The scientific insight driving our solution is the unique ability of mushroom mycelium to break down lignocellulosic agricultural waste while producing nutrient-dense food and beneficial soil microorganisms. Our process involves:  1. Collection and preprocessing of rice straw using our established procurement network 2. Specialized substrate preparation optimized for dual-purpose cultivation 3. Production of gourmet mushrooms as a nutritious food source 4. Processing of spent substrate to develop mycorrhizal-enhanced soil amendments  This solution delivers multiple immediate benefits:  - Farmers receive income from crop residue instead of burning it - Local communities gain access to affordable, protein-rich mushrooms - Soil health improves through mycorrhizal amendments - Air quality benefits from reduced stubble burning  The sustainable benefits include:  - Creation of a circular agricultural economy - Enhanced soil carbon sequestration - Improved crop yields through better soil health - Reduced dependence on chemical fertilizers

Project Title: KENYA MARA   Regenerating Traditional Foods, Lands & Livelihoods through Maasai Conservancies
Executive Summary: GFSC funding will help regenerate 100,000 hectares of communally-managed Maasai conservancies in Kenya s Mara region. Through the scaling of ongoing, successful implementation of Holistic Management, this project is helping Maasai herders incorporate regenerative practices into traditional livelihoods. This project will increase resilience for 8,000+ people through improved land health, food security and nutrition, and tourism-driven income, all while restoring iconic wildlife habitat of the Maasai Mara and sequestering ~180K tons of carbon.
Innovation Description: The Maasai have historically been pastoralists, relying on a traditional diet primarily composed of blood, milk, and meat. However, since the 1950s when British colonial administration imposed restrictions on cattle grazing, a substantial number have been pushed to transition to government-supported farming programs, leading to a replacement of traditional dietary staples with maize, grains, and cereals, and subsequently to notable increases in both BMI and diabetes (Pressier et al. 2022).   Addressing these challenges is integral to our project's mission, which is empowering the Maasai to regenerate land-health and productivity through Holistic Management which, in turn, contributes to improved nutritional well-being by bolstering access to traditional animal-based dietary staples and improving livestock health. While research evaluating associations between land health and food s nutrient density is still in its infancy, Provenza et al. 2019 notes that  circumstantial evidence supports the hypothesis that phytochemical richness of herbivore diets enhances biochemical richness of meat and dairy, which is linked with human and environmental health.  By enhancing forage biodiversity through properly-managed grazing, the Maasai will simultaneously enhance nutrient density of traditional foods. Further, widespread exclusion of people and livestock from designated  conservation areas,  driven by colonial and post-colonial policies and economic forces, has led to significant reductions in grassland productivity with numerous consequences such as diminished livelihoods and associated social challenges, and diminished wildlife habitat and associated tourism income.  This project is implemented through conservancies, where livestock is holistically-managed by pastoralists to regenerate land health, presenting a win-win solution for both environmental and socioeconomic outcomes.

Project Title: YieldSync: Precision Agriculture, Perfectly Timed
Executive Summary: YieldSync is an innovative GeoAI-powered suite of digital tools revolutionizing agriculture. It combines advanced satellite imagery, 17 specialized indices and machine learning to optimize productivity, sustainability and resilience. With features like grid-based scoring, yield estimation (macro and micro) and global carbon credit modeling through BiomeSync, YieldSync empowers stakeholders with actionable insights. Designed for scalability, it addresses inefficiencies, reduces environmental impact and fosters food security, with global pilots set for Q1 2025.
Innovation Description: YieldSync addresses critical challenges in agriculture, including inefficiency, yield variability, environmental degradation, and a lack of precise tools for informed decision-making. Traditional practices often rely on intuition and static data, leaving farmers and stakeholders ill-equipped to tackle complex issues like climate variability, resource mismanagement, and unsustainable practices. These inefficiencies contribute to food insecurity, economic instability, and environmental harm.  YieldSync offers a transformative solution with four integrated components:  Agricultural Excellence Tools: Using 17 indices, YieldSync generates classified maps, time-series data, and actionable insights for resource optimization. AgriShield AI: A patented (application in progress) system employing grid-based scoring, dynamic recommendations, and geospatial analytics to monitor and improve farm performance. Yield Estimation System: Macro-level predictions support regional planning, while micro-level tools offer plot-specific yield forecasts to guide precise interventions. BiomeSync: A carbon credit estimation platform, currently under patent discussions and validation with leading organizations, quantifies carbon sequestration, enabling sustainable practices and financial incentives for farmers. This innovation combines advanced geospatial technologies, machine learning and environmental insights, offering immediate benefits such as improved yields, efficient resource use and data-driven decision-making for farmers. Its sustainable impact extends to society and the environment by reducing carbon footprints, enhancing food security and fostering resilient agricultural ecosystems. YieldSync empowers users to navigate global agricultural challenges with cutting-edge tools and actionable insights, driving meaningful change in the industry.

Project Title: Development of non-toxic oxygen absorbers to prolong food shelf life
Executive Summary: We are developing non-iron-based oxygen absorbers for the prolonging of food shelf life. We already have a minimum viable product with our patented technology called the MSN (Mesoporous Silica Nanosphere). This is a non-toxic, bio-compatible alternative to existing products in the market. We are also developing a film-based product that could be applied on fresh harvests. Our next step is to scale up by finding suppliers and clients for our products.
Innovation Description: Food loss and waste present a significant global challenge, with one-third of all food produced lost to spoilage. A substantial portion of this occurs during post-harvest and storage before reaching consumers. Current preservation methods for processed foods typically reduce oxygen levels to only 0.5   2 vol%, which still leads to deterioration over time. Additionally, preserving fresh fruits poses a major challenge, affecting food availability and causing considerable economic losses and environmental waste.  Our patented technology utilizing mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSNs) offers a faster, safer, and more efficient solution for oxygen absorption in food preservation. Our oxygen scavengers can effectively reduce oxygen levels to 0.1 vol% in packaging headspace, which is optimal for maintaining food quality. Unlike traditional iron-based absorbers, our solution is biocompatible, ensuring safety for consumers.  We are also developing a film-based product that incorporates MSN technology. Currently in the proof-of-concept stage, this innovation adapts to the specific respiration and transpiration rates of the produce, naturally achieving equilibrium gas concentrations within the packaging to extend shelf life.  Both our sachet-based and film-based products can significantly prolong the freshness of food items, benefiting food companies by minimizing economic losses and providing consumers with safer preservation options. Ultimately, our technology contributes to reducing food waste, leading to less environmental impact and promoting a more sustainable food cycle.

Project Title: Nourishing a Sustainable Future: Regenerative Agriculture for Affordable, Healthy, and Climate-Resilient Food Systems
Executive Summary: Our project will support 2,000 smallholder farmers (SHF) adopt regenerative agriculture (RA) practices by offering training, practical support, and incorporating resilience-building initiatives, enabling a sustainable transition that increases biodiversity, restores soil health, and mitigate climate change. This will also improve access to affordable, sustainably grown, nutritious food and promote healthier diets.
Innovation Description: Our innovation is transforming the food-production system in sub-Saharan Africa by enabling SHFs to become economically & environmentally resilient. We do this by building a scalable and financially self-sustaining business model that transitions SHFs to regenerative farming and providing assured income increase leading to economic transformation (income increase), biodiverse farms, while improving food security & diets. We make money through the offtake and subsides the cost of training & production through the margins from that.    The problem we set out to solve is that of SHFs being economically and environmentally vulnerable. SHFs in sub-Saharan Africa are classified as extremely poor ( 1.5 USD/day) and their situation is expected to worsen   with accelerating climate change, dropping productivity of land due to unsustainable practices, and already being food insecure   and they are wholly unprepared for this. There are an estimated 5M SHF in Kenya (and 500M in sub-Saharan Africa) who face this problem, leading to unprecedented food insecurity & climate migration.    Regenerative agriculture provides a slow take-back of biodiversity, improved yields, improved nutrition, and improved incomes. It has been proven in desert landscapes and arid regions to regenerate plants, soils, animals, and insects critical to a healthy ecosystem. We would like to replicate this at the SHF level in a way that is economically and commercially viable both to the SHF and our scalable business model

Project Title: KaFresh: Feeding the Next Billion
Executive Summary: Sio Valley Technologies' project, Feeding the Next Billion, is designed to expand the use of KaFresh in existing markets and reach new regions both across Africa and beyond. The project will support the growth of SVT's sales team and increase end user awareness of KaFresh through strong marketing campaigns and promotional events. The project will allow SVT to establish lasting impact evaluation and quality control measures.
Innovation Description: SVT is solving the lack of efficient post-harvest management systems in Africa, where 40-60% of harvested crops are lost annually due to spoilage caused by pests, mold, and moisture. SVT focuses on post-harvest management in Sub-Saharan Africa because food spoilage not only represents a major financial cost but also a grave humanitarian concern. Approximately 1.3 billion tons of food are wasted or lost globally each year, equating to $940 billion (FAO 2021), while about 735 million people face hunger (FAO, 2022). SVT's first to market product, KaFresh, significantly reduces these losses which enhances food availability, eases pressure on resources, combats hunger, and provides pathways to improved farmer livelihood.   KaFresh is an innovative solution using a proprietary blend of natural ingredients to extend the shelf life of fruits and vegetables at room temperature by up to 500%, eliminating the need for expensive cold storage solutions. KaFresh's technology creates a very thin, edible coating that inhibits cell wall breakdown and regulates respiration rate & ethylene production, slowing down the ripening process.   Additionally, KaFresh empowers farmers by democratizing access to food storage technologies, enabling them to grow their income through reduced post-harvest losses and improved produce quality at market.  By minimizing spoilage, KaFresh combats food waste, in turn reducing GHG emission from landfills. Ultimately, this enhances food security and promotes a more sustainable food system within communities.

Project Title: Enhancing Food Safety Through Affordable Quality Testing Kits for SMEs.
Executive Summary: This project aims to develop affordable, portable food testing kits tailored for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to ensure compliance with global food safety standards. These kits will test for contaminants like heavy metals, pesticides, and microbial pathogens, empowering SMEs to produce safer food products while reducing costs and reliance on third-party testing facilities. The initiative promotes accessibility, sustainability, and global food security.
Innovation Description: Innovation Description: The project introduces affordable, portable food testing kits designed to help SMEs ensure food safety by detecting contaminants like heavy metals, pesticides, and microbial pathogens. These kits address the high cost and inaccessibility of laboratory testing, which often hinders SMEs from complying with food safety standards. Problem and Relevance: Food safety is a critical issue globally, with unsafe food causing illnesses, economic losses, and reduced consumer confidence. SMEs, particularly in developing regions, struggle with costly testing and lack of access to certified laboratories, leading to undetected hazards in their products. This gap in quality assurance affects public health and limits market access for these producers. Solution: The portable kits leverage advances in biosensor technology, immunoassays, and colorimetric detection to offer reliable, user-friendly, and cost-effective testing. They allow producers to test raw materials and finished products on-site, ensuring compliance with food safety standards without expensive equipment or specialized training. Scientific Insight: The solution draws on research in rapid, field-deployable diagnostic tools, which combine sensitivity, specificity, and simplicity. These innovations address the unique needs of SMEs by reducing dependency on third-party facilities. Benefits: Immediate benefits include safer food, reduced production costs, and increased market access for SMEs. Long-term, the kits empower communities, improve public health, and promote sustainability by reducing foodborne illnesses. This innovation supports farmers, producers, schools, and society by making food safety accessible, fostering trust in local products, and contributing to a safer global food supply chain.

Project Title: Healthy Climate & Fresh Food for All
Executive Summary: Sky High Farm works to ensure everyone has access to the resources they need to sustain themselves, including nutrient-dense, culturally-appropriate food. Simultaneously, we seek to improve the ecological integrity of a large plot of conventionally farmed land with climate-forward farming methods (including soil health studies, native grasses and pollinator protection) while providing high-quality meat, eggs, and produce to those in our community suffering food insecurity.
Innovation Description: In 2020, amidst the COVID-19 pandemic, food insecurity was exacerbated for our region's most marginalized communities, with many families and individuals facing insufficiency for the first time. Layered on the cascading issues of the pandemic, we are also facing untenable food prices due to inflation. Our responsibility to provide culturally relevant, high-quality vegetables, meat, and eggs to our community not only for free, but on a consistent year-round basis, has become increasingly urgent in recent years. We recognize the serious consequences of environmental racism and how the climate crisis most impacts marginalized communities. In this context, we are committed to regenerative farming practices that honor the land, prioritize the health of our farmers, and produce quality food with minimal inputs. These practices work to counterbalance the harm of industrial farming, while giving our environment and our people the care they deserve. To accomplish this, we are planting a variety of cover crops into former corn and soy fields to address soil health improvement in advance of planned native grass and wildflower plantings. Ultimately, we will establish a perennial stand of native plants for pollinator habitat and grazing beef cattle, promoting pasture diversity and restoring soil health on nearly 200 acres of perennial pasture. This work is a reflection of our deeply held belief and responsibility to not only feed our community, but to do so in a way that cares for the long lasting impacts on our neighbors and the future of our planet.

Project Title: Innovative Peanut Root-Breaking Technology for Sustainable and Efficient Post-Harvest Farming
Executive Summary: Our Peanut Root-Breaker Machine reduces the tedious peanut harvesting process from 8 12 hours of manual labor per acre to just 3 4 hours. Traditionally, farmers spend long hours sitting and separating peanuts by hand, a slow and exhausting task. Our machine cuts labor costs by 40% reduces post-harvest losses by 30%, and increases efficiency. By leasing at TZS 3,000 per sack, we aim to transform peanut farming for 5 million farmers in Tanzania.
Innovation Description: Innovation: Skyverse Solutions has developed a peanut root-breaking machine that revolutionizes the peanut post-harvest process. It simplifies the traditionally labor-intensive and time-consuming task of separating peanuts from roots and branches, improving the efficiency of peanut harvesting for smallholder farmers.  Problem: In Tanzania, over 5 million smallholder peanut farmers face challenges with high post-harvest losses (up to 30%) due to outdated separation methods, which are time-consuming, labor-intensive, and costly. Traditional methods can take up to 15 minutes per sack, leading to long working hours and significant labor costs.  Solution: The peanut root-breaking machine reduces the time required for separation to just 4-5 minutes per sack, cutting harvesting time from 8-12 hours per acre to 3-4 hours per acre. This saves 50% of time and reduces labor costs by 40%. The machine also reduces post-harvest losses by making the separation process more efficient.  Scientific Insight: The design leverages mechanical engineering principles to effectively break the peanut roots in bundles, enabling faster collection and separation. It s built with a focus on affordability and sustainability, allowing farmers to lease it at a cost-effective rate.  Benefits: Farmers benefit from reduced labor costs and increased productivity, leading to higher profits. Environmental impact is positive as fewer peanuts are wasted, and sustainable farming practices are promoted. Communities gain through improved food security and enhanced local economies. This innovation is a scalable solution that can drive long-term change in Tanzania s agricultural sector.

Project Title: Accelerating Agricultural Food Production Consumption and Market Access for Resilient Food Systems in Northern Uganda
Executive Summary: The project Accelerating Agricultural Food Production Consumption and Market Access for Resilient Food Systems in Northern Uganda" by Slow Food Uganda aims to transition towards sustainable agricultural practices, improve local farmers livelihoods and increase consumer awareness of agroecological foods. The project is designed to  transition local communities toward agroecological practices, which focus on sustainable, environmentally friendly food production while improving livelihoods. The innovation lies in integrating agroecology into farming practices and value chains through initiatives such as establishing  Earth Markets, seed banks, and agroecology knowledge centers. Earth  Markets connect farmers directly with consumers, enabling  fair prices and improved incomes for over 1,000 households. Seed banks  preserve and promote local crop diversity, enhancing food security and resilience against climate variability. Knowledge centers and  training programs equip farmers and local  trainers with skills in  sustainable agriculture, financial literacy, value addition, and marketing. For consumers, the  project raises awareness about the health and nutritional benefits of organically grown foods through media campaigns, cross-learning  events, and partnerships with chefs and restaurants. These activities encourage a shift in purchasing habits toward  healthier, locally produced foods, benefiting over  2,000 people. By fostering stronger  value chains, the project creates immediate benefits for farmers, schools, and communities while ensuring long-term sustainability for  society and the environment. It provides a replicable model  for sustainable food systems in Northern Uganda.

Project Title: Transforming Food Security with IoT-Smart Hydroponic Systems for Sustainable and Climate-Resilient Agriculture
Executive Summary: Smartel leverages IoT technology to enhance hydroponic farming, offering sustainable solutions with sensors that identify plant defects, manage risks, and enable remote cultivation in any location. Our systems use 100% organic nutrients, reducing costs, enhancing productivity, and minimizing water use and carbon emissions. Targeting urban farmers, we mitigate post-harvest losses through IoT-enabled remote control and real-time monitoring, ensuring fresh, nutritious produce is grown efficiently in any location, while promoting environmentally friendly farming practices.
Innovation Description: Smartel designs, builds, and deploys portable IoT-smart hydroponic systems to disrupt traditional farming. Our systems utilize sensors to identify plant defects, manage risks through early warning signs, and enable the cultivation of fresh produce remotely and in any location. Unlike conventional hydroponic systems, ours operates on green energy 24/7, ensuring sustainable functionality. We address the dual challenges of food insecurity and unsustainable agricultural practices. Our innovation solves the problem of limited arable land, water scarcity, and nutritional deficiencies by enabling year-round cultivation of fresh produce with 90% less water and 100% organic nutrients. This is increasingly relevant as climate change impacts traditional farming, driving up the need for affordable, sustainable food solutions. Our hydroponic systems allow real-time monitoring, empowering farmers to detect plant defects and optimize resource use. Built on the principles of soilless farming and enhanced by IoT for precision agriculture, our solution targets urban and peri-urban farmers, reducing post-harvest losses through localized, controlled production. Immediate benefits include fresh, nutritious produce addressing dietary deficiencies, especially in children, while farmers achieve higher yields at lower costs. Long-term benefits include reducing carbon emissions, conserving water, and restoring soil. Each system we build reduces 1.2 metric tons of CO₂ emissions annually. Farmers are integrated into our value chains, receiving training and market access. Smartel empowers communities to thrive, creating a sustainable and equitable model for food production while safeguarding the planet. Our innovation transforms agriculture into a catalyst for equity, health, and resilience.

Project Title: Addressing climate change by growing fruit and native trees in dry & degraded lands using carbon sink planters.
Executive Summary: . Our initiative  manufactures and promotes application of carbon-sink planters a low-cost, biodegradable  packaging in which trees can grow autonomously with minimal irrigation and sell-affordably to  subsistence farmers/private commercial farms willing to plant trees in dry lands. Carbon sink  planters is a packaging for olivine sand (one ton of olivine sand can take in up to one ton of  CO2) and other rock minerals like diatomite with high water retention advantages blended  with solid food waste which is first modified into bio-char. Our initiative utilises chemical,  physical, and biological modification processes that improves the agronomic effectiveness of  food waste to produce bio-char. Bio-char is also an efficient form of carbon sequestration, are  hygroscopic and can retain water and soluble nutrients to be released slowly over time.  Carbon sink planters allows trees to grow in soil that would otherwise not be conducive to  growth and as it breaks down provides healthy microorganism life and an environment that is  healthier for plant life due to introduction of shade and increased water retention in the soil  among other factors. Carbon sink planters for growing trees acts as an agent for soil  improvement, improved resource use efficiency, remediation and/or protection against  environmental pollution and as an avenue for greenhouse gas (GHG) mitigation.

The solar dryers are energy-efficient, climate-friendly, and tailored to local conditions, making them a sustainable solution for food processing in resource-constrained settings. By combining cutting-edge technology with fair trade practices and local expertise, the project delivers lasting benefits for farmers, communities, and the environment while paving the way for regional market expansion.

Project Title: Transnational Black Women s Food Sovereignty Re-Imaging & Re-Imagining
Executive Summary: This photography-based project connects Black women gardeners in Mwanza, Tanzania to Black Indigenous Garifuna sustenance farmers in Punta Piedra, Honduras. Connecting through images of women s farms, gardens, and food, these women will see the beauty and feel the inspiration of Black women s efforts to provide their communities with fresh, healthy food. Through a website-based photo gallery and social media campaign, Black women globally will be invited to share their connections to land and food.
Innovation Description: Language is often a barrier when people share their stories. However, photography is a universal language that can communicate across the barriers of spoken language, providing a sense of deep connection. In many countries, Black (and Indigenous) women are marginalized in (patriarchal) stories of (white or mestizo male) farmers and their strength. This photography and social media campaign intends to support a #TransnationalBlackWomensFoodSovereignty social media that highlights the difficult and beautiful labor that is behind Black women s efforts to provide their families and communities with fresh, healthy meals.   By leveraging social media technologies to share images, we will shift the image (and ultimately the narrative) around Black women s agricultural labor and relationship to fresh produce. Too often, Black communities (especially in non-Black majority countries) are stereotyped as eating fried and unhealthy foods. These stereotypes result in discrimination against Black women and inattention to (non-diet-related) health concerns. This project will show encourage and inspire Black women s global connections to each other and gardening and farming with fruits and vegetables.  The project will focus on two communities of Black women on different continents. They will share their local traditions, closing the distance between them with the power of mobile technology. The immediate benefits are pride in the agricultural and food traditions of these communities that will inspire broader appreciation of their contributions to food sovereignty and greater encouragement among women. In the best case scenario, what begins as a year-long campaign will become a viral social media trend.

Project Title: Ikemon Green Rural Community: Agro-Business Incubation, Training, Seeding, Networking, and Services to empower West African youth's socio-economic development.
Executive Summary: This proposal establishes the "Ikemon Green Rural Community" in Benin as a sustainable agro-food hub, technology park, and incubation center for West African youth. Using the integrated Songhai model, it will train 2,000 youth in the region in regenerative agriculture, biotechnology, and IT, creating ecosystems for systemic growth, wealth, and employment. The initiative combats soil degradation, restores productivity with climate-smart practices, and leverages IT and biotechnology to unlock regional potential within a transformative $500,000 budget.
Innovation Description: Songhai s innovative approach represents a groundbreaking, zero-waste agricultural ecosystem that seamlessly integrates regenerative agriculture, sustainable technology, and community empowerment to address Africa s most pressing food system challenges. This dynamic model not only combats poverty, unemployment, and food insecurity but also reverses land degradation, positioning agriculture as a transformative engine for socio-economic and ecological progress. At its core, the Songhai model synergizes three interconnected sectors: the primary sector (a harmonized system of crop production, livestock, and aquaculture), the secondary sector (value addition through agro-processing and renewable energy solutions), and the tertiary sector (market access enhanced by digital platforms). By closing resource loops and recycling organic by-products, it achieves unparalleled efficiency, reducing dependency on harmful chemical inputs while fostering environmental resilience. We produce more and better with less. Rooted in scientific principles of biomimicry and circular economies, Songhai employs environmentally friendly  practices such as agroforestry, polyculture, and soil regeneration to restore soil fertility, enhance biodiversity, and mitigate climate change. Cutting-edge technologies like IoT sensors, solar-powered systems, and e-commerce platforms further amplify productivity, streamline supply chains, and connect farmers to markets in real time. This paradigm creates immediate benefits higher yields, lower costs, and expanded job opportunities for youth and women while establishing a foundation for long-term impact: empowered communities, equitable food access, and a reinvigorated ecological balance. For consumers, it ensures affordable, nutritious food, aligning with sustainable practices that protect planetary health. Songhai s integrative model offers a scalable blueprint for sustainable, resilient, and inclusive food systems, capable of transforming Africa and inspiring global change.

Project Title: Ensuring food security for migrant families in Turkana, Kenya and Ciudad Juarez, Mexico using AI precision and regenerative agriculture practices
Executive Summary: Building on pilot activities, our project will expand regenerative agriculture and AI precision farming practices. Working with experienced partners and migrants/refugees in shelters and camps, in Ciudad Juarez, Mexico and Turkana County, Kenya, our aim is to increase and diversify production to secure healthy diets, provide participants with life skills, and share learning widely.  New tools will maximize crop yields, improve nutritional status and reduce water use, leading to more sustainable food systems
Innovation Description: South North Nexus (SNN) works in two similar geographical locations with refugees and migrants. The camps and shelters are situated in dry ecosystems that face many challenges, including food and nutrition insecurity and access to clean water due to harsh climatic conditions, minimal rainfall and limited infrastructure. The food and nutrition challenges faced by refugees in Kakuma Camp in Turkana County, Kenya include lack of nutritious foods, including fruits, vegetables and insufficient proteins. The camp is home to almost 300,000 people, with many settlements. The other location is Ciudad Juarez, a U.S. Mexico border point of entry for asylum seekers. In border shelters, food and nutrition security depends heavily on the church community to provide donations to cover basic food and water needs. Most shelter residents are fleeing violence and political instability. SNN has been partnering in both locations for the last three years, introducing practices that allow residents to participate in growing nutritious foods. Women are significant players in food production however, they still lack access to farming skills and new agricultural technologies.  With a focus on sharing technologies and learning, the project will integrate AI and regenerative practices with: 1) HOBOware to monitor soil humidity, temperature, dissolved nutrients and pH; 2) solar-powered pumping systems, including for irrigation; and 3) indigenous crops, using agroforestry techniques among other practices. Training topics for families, local officials and stakeholders, will include: tool use and maintenance, nutrition, agriculture practices and financial literacy. Special attention will be given to women s skill enhancement.

Project Title: From farms to global stages: Telling the Untold Stories of Women in Agriculture.
Executive Summary: "From Farms to Global Stages" is a transformative project by Spring Agric aimed at empowering women farmers by amplifying their untold stories. Through storytelling, media campaigns, and training, the initiative will elevate women s leadership in agriculture, promote climate-smart and sustainable farming, and build global networks for advocacy. This project seeks to increase visibility, provide resources, and influence policies, ultimately enhancing the economic empowerment and resilience of women farmers while contributing to sustainable food systems worldwide.
Innovation Description: Innovation Description:  Spring Agric is introducing a holistic approach to empower women farmers through climate-smart agriculture, agroecology, and value addition practices. The project focuses on providing women with the tools, training, and market access needed to boost agricultural productivity, reduce post-harvest losses, and increase resilience to climate change. Problem Being Solved: Agriculture in Kenya is highly vulnerable to climate change, with women, who make up 80% of smallholder farmers, facing increased challenges such as crop failures, water scarcity, and soil degradation. Additionally, women often lack access to resources, information, and markets, which hinders their economic potential and food security. Solution: Spring Agric addresses these issues by training women farmers in sustainable farming practices, including water conservation, soil fertility management, and crop diversification. The integration of value-added products such as dried fruits and flours reduces post-harvest losses and increases income. The use of mobile technology provides real-time climate data, market updates, and farming tips, enhancing decision-making and productivity. Scientific/Technical Insight: The solution is based on agroecology and climate-smart agriculture principles, which emphasize soil health, water conservation, and biodiversity. Leveraging digital tools ensures farmers receive timely information to adapt to changing conditions, improving their ability to respond to climate shocks. Immediate and Sustainable Benefits: Increased yields and income for farmers through sustainable practices. Reduced post-harvest losses, ensuring more food for communities. Improved food security and nutritional diversity. Empowered women who become leaders in their communities. Enhanced environmental resilience by promoting eco-friendly farming practices.

Project Title: Dynamic Sprouting: Sustainable AI-Driven Superfood Production
Executive Summary: Our project is design and development of AI-driven, automated mini-factories to produce nutrient-rich, safe sprouted superfoods sustainably. Using  3L water/kg, no pesticides, and eliminating biohazards, these scalable factories reduce emissions and offer 2-6x more bioavailable superfoods locally. Targeting the $12B global superfood market, our innovation addresses critical needs in nutrition, food safety, and sustainability.
Innovation Description: Sprout Dynamics addresses critical challenges in food safety, malnutrition, sustainability, and scalability through AI-driven mini-factories for sprouting seeds. These automated systems use  3L water/kg, require no pesticides, and eliminate biohazards like salmonella via real-time AI monitoring, producing safe and affordable superfoods.  Problem Solved  Malnutrition and Chronic Illness: Limited access to safe, nutrient-dense food. Scalability Issues: Current sprouting is an artisanal $5B industry, lacking scalable and mass-production solutions. Resource Inefficiency: High water, pesticide, and land use in traditional agriculture. Food Safety: Biohazards like salmonella and mold in conventional sprouting processes. Vegetarian Nutrition Gaps: Lack of plant-based omega-3 sources; sprouts offer a sustainable, nutrient-rich alternative to fish.  Target Groups and Benefits  B2B (Food Producers & Retail Chains): Affordable, scalable solutions for producing nutrient-rich superfoods. Opportunities to launch products like frozen sprout mixes, meeting consumer health trends.  B2B2C (Resellers & Supermarkets): Expanded product portfolios with high-nutrition, sustainable options. Access to scalable, mass-produced sprouted seeds for growing superfood demand.  Diabetes Patients and Associations: Low glycemic, high-fiber foods for managing blood sugar levels. Tailored products for specialized dietary needs.  Vegetarians: A sustainable, plant-based omega-3 source with flaxseed sprouts, rich in alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) and essential nutrients. Nutritional replacement for fish with high bioavailability of fiber, protein, and fatty acids.  Chefs and Food Innovators: Unlimited creative possibilities with nutrient-dense sprouted ingredients. Consistent supply of safe, high-quality seeds for culinary innovation.  Communities and Schools: Affordable, healthy meals improving dietary outcomes. Local, decentralized production ensures food security and reduces transportation emissions.

Project Title: Innovative Students  Engagement in Nutritious Food Production, Preservation and Processing in Uganda
Executive Summary: The project empowers Students to engage in Nutritious Food Production, Preservation and Processing (NFPPP) through operating; a. smart-urban gardening of nutritious vegetables; supported by solar-irrigation and composting for bio-fertilizers; b. post-harvest food preservation and processing; c. rearing chicken, pigs, rabbits and fish; enabled by recycled food-waste and black-soldier-fly-larvae. Recycling redeems over 768 tons of food-waste generated daily (in Kampala city alone) and facilitates the bridging of the current nutrient deficits in schools and communities.
Innovation Description: Students in average Ugandan schools lack sufficient nutrients; only 28% energy needs, 64% proteins, 40% vitamins, and 42% iron. The deficiency, which affects health and academic productivity, is caused by high costs of nutritious foods attributed to post-harvest food loss and waste (FLW) along the critical value chains. For instance, between 30%   50% of harvested fruits and vegetables and 20-25% of root-crops are lost annually (Fingo 2023). Small and medium-level farmers stockpile their harvests because of lack of basic skills and technologies for postharvest handling, food preservation and processing (FAO 2019; Viola 2017). FLW is associated with foodborne illnesses and food poisoning (caused by aflatoxins, molding and microbial pathogens). Part of the project activities is to skill students to engage in availing nutrient-rich human feeds through operating two types of projects; 1. Producing nutritious food components whose specific activities include; a. smart-urban farming of vegetables (mushrooms, onions, tomatoes, variety of greens); b. producing organic pesticides; c. composting for bio-fertilizers; d. rearing chicken, rabbits, fish, and pigs (off-campus); e. food-waste recycling and black-soldier-fly-larvae rearing (to secure nutrient-rich feeds for the livestock); 2. Post-harvest food preservation and processing whose activities include; a. food processing/preservation via shredding, drying, heat-sterilization; b. food fortification (mixing various nutrient components); c. generating clean energy (solar and briquettes) to power preservation and processing processes. Besides boosting nutrition, the project promotes circularity and enhances environmental sustainability. The green entrepreneurship nurtured by the project enables income generation and job creation along food production and distribution value chain.

Project Title: A Community Bakehouse: Transforming Lives through Social Enterprise
Executive Summary: The proposed Bakehouse will produce nutritious snacks, buns, biscuits, cakes, and bread using millets like ragi, bajra, and whole wheat. It aims to 1) support immune-compromised care home children, infants, and patients, 2) offer baking and entrepreneurship training for rural youth, especially women, and 3) provide affordable, healthy baked goods for the rural community. This initiative fosters nutritional awareness and community empowerment while establishing a sustainable social enterprise.
Innovation Description: St. Gregorios Dayabhavan prioritizes food security to support immune-compromised care home children, HIV/AIDS patients, infants, and caregiving staff. Additionally, it serves 425 non-residential children from rural, disease-affected households, providing meals, education, and medicines. Beyond the campus, nearly 10,000 beneficiaries, including slum dwellers, elderly poor, and migrants in Tumkur district, receive dry food kits and meal parcels as part of its community outreach.  This project aims to produce nutritious snacks buns, cakes, biscuits, and bread using millet-based ingredients like ragi and jowar. It will address hunger relief and dietary needs while promoting a healthy diet. Rural women will play key roles in food production, packaging, and sales, gaining entrepreneurial skills and fostering a sustainable social enterprise model.  The initiative involves installing baking equipment dough mixers, ovens, bread slicer, chiller, and storage facilities in a 1,625 sq. ft. existing building at the Kunigal campus. Automation ensures hygienic, fatigue-free operations, minimizes waste and simplifies processes for rural women. The production will meet the needs of care home residents and disease-affected families while generating a surplus for affordable sales to rural households and nearby communities.  With low operational costs and energy-efficient tools, the project ensures economic viability and scalability. Cost estimates are USD 19910 (kitchen equipment, stipend for trainees, food license) with a 12-month timeline. The project will serve over 10,000 beneficiaries annually, fulfilling a mandate of community service while fostering nutrition awareness and economic empowerment.

Project Title: Sustaining Village Livelihood Project
Website: Website still under development. Facebook page: https://www.facebook.com/suerydermalawi
Executive Summary: The project will provide a start-up flock of five goats, and a package of mindset change sessions to 20 vulnerable families. When the goats reproduce, the initial beneficiaries will pass the off-springs and skills to another set of 20 households who will also pass on the off-spring and skills until all the ultra-poor households are reached. The Project will promote use of goat dung to produce organic fertilizer for use in beneficiaries fields.
Innovation Description: According to the 2018 Population and Housing Census, Balaka District s poverty level is at 66.9% against the national incidence of 58.8%. Between 2010 and 2019, the contribution of agriculture as the main source of household-level income declined from 70% to below 50% (Escaping Poverty in Malawi Requires Improved Agricultural Productivity, Climate Resilience, and Structural Transformation - World Bank . Ironically, information about weather forecasts does not reach the communities, and they end up cultivating crops which do not fit into the weather pattern for the particular year thereby experiencing perpetual food insecurity. Additionally, ultra-poor households have challenges in adopting other livelihood options such as animal husbandry because of both affordability and mindset factors. Malawi Government effects unconditional social cash transfers to ultra-poor households in order to cater for basic needs. However, about two thirds of the households 73% for the Comparison group) have transfer shares of less than 20 percent, which is considered the recommended level for expecting widespread impacts (Malawi Social Cash Transfer Programme Longitudinal Impact Evaluation: Baseline Report, December 2022). Even so, SCTP beneficiaries are usually prevented from accessing additional humanitarian support on the pretext that they should let others benefit as well. The project will support ultra-poor households including women and persons with disabilities with goats, mindset change sessions and support towards climate-smart agriculture practices, so that they should transition to more secure livelihoods, and start building their asset base. Project Title: An outreach project: Leveraging circularity in fish farming through BSFL production using horticultural waste.
Website: Currently we are still developing website
Executive Summary: The proposed project is intended to promote fish farming through the application of circularity principles. The project aimed at empowering farmers; enhance waste management by conducting outreach activities. Specifically, a demonstration model on Black Soldier fly larvae (BSFL) production and fish farming will be developed, farmers will be trained and finally extension manual and policy brief will be developed. Production of fish using BSFL produced using organic waste will increase fish while maintaining clean environment.
Innovation Description: One of the challenges facing the aquaculture sector is the excessive cost of feed. The production of black soldier fly larvae will function as an alternative source of feed protein. Research has been conducted on the production, applicability, and benefits of black soldier fly larvae using circular economy principles. Different bio-waste has been used in BSFL using livestock manure (Dzepe et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2013), crop residues (Mutafela, 2015), and brewery waste (Eggink et al., 2022). BSFL has been used in aquaculture, poultry feed, and waste management. Despite voluminous scientific publications on the production and use of BSFL, small-scale fish farmers and environmental officers are not conversant in the production of BSFL and its advantages in animal nutrition and waste management. The proposed project is intended to use the existing scientific knowledge to address the future challenge of food and environment using innovative outreach activities. Immediate benefits include reduced feeding expenses for farmers, improved farm profitability, and a clean environment. Long-term sustainable benefits include reduced reliance on fishmeal and lower carbon footprints in aquaculture operations. The beneficiaries of this project will include fish farmers, poultry keepers, extension agents, environmental officers, and the community at large. Fish farmers and poultry keepers will benefit from access to affordable, high-quality black soldier fly larvae (BSFL) feed. Extension agents will gain knowledge and tools to promote sustainable aquaculture practices, while environmental officers will benefit from improved waste management. It is envisaged that this project will contribute significantly to food security.

Project Title: Empowering Communities with Sustainable Food: Mushroom Grow Blocks and Free Bareroot Plant Distribution
Executive Summary: Our project provides free oyster mushroom grow blocks and bareroot starts of herbs, berries, vegetables, and fruit trees to communities. By building a greenhouse for propagation and distribution, we aim to nourish families, teach sustainable food cultivation, and promote self-sufficiency. Partnering with schools, churches, missions, and community groups, we empower individuals to grow their own nutritious food, fostering healthier communities and addressing food insecurity sustainably.
Innovation Description: Our innovation addresses food insecurity by combining sustainable food cultivation with community empowerment, aligning with the Seeding The Future Global Food System Challenge. By providing free oyster mushroom grow blocks and bareroot starts of herbs, berries, vegetables, and fruit trees, we empower individuals and families to grow their own nutritious food, fostering self-sufficiency and reducing reliance on external sources. Solution: Our ready-to-fruit oyster mushroom grow blocks are nutrient-dense, fast-growing, and easy to use. Bareroot plants diversify food options and ensure long-term sustainability. Oyster mushrooms, rich in protein, essential amino acids, B-vitamins, and minerals, improve diets while requiring minimal resources. A greenhouse will support year-round propagation and distribution, increasing food security in underserved areas.  Scientific and Technical Insights: Oyster mushrooms efficiently convert agricultural waste into nutrient-dense food within weeks. Bareroot plants, propagated during dormancy, adapt well to diverse climates and optimize water and nutrient uptake, supporting localized food production and resilience.  Alignment with Challenge Goals:  Transformational Impact: Empowers communities to address food insecurity sustainably. Sustainability and Health: Promotes eco-friendly cultivation and reduces waste. Equitable Access: Ensures fresh, nutritious food for underserved populations.  This scalable solution fosters sustainable food systems, improves nutrition, and builds community resilience.

Project Title: Smart Solar Dryers: Empowering Smallholder Farmers by Reducing Post- Harvest Losses and Boosting Nutrition.
Executive Summary: Smart Solar Dryers use solar-powered HVAC systems and IoT sensors to reduce post-harvest losses by 40%, preserve nutrients, and improve crop quality. Through the Rent-to-Dry model, it offers affordable dryer services, enabling value addition and transforming surplus harvests into high-value products. This technology lowers carbon emissions, boosts farmer incomes, and strengthens food systems while supporting sustainable livelihoods and improved nutrition, particularly for youth and women smallholder farmers in agro-processing.
Innovation Description: The project aims to improve food safety, nutrient retention, and access to healthful diets by addressing post-harvest inefficiencies across agri-value chains. It reduces spoilage, enables value addition, and ensures that high-quality, nutritious food reaches consumers while enhancing the livelihoods of smallholder farmers in rural Kenya. Traditional drying methods, such as sun drying, expose produce to inconsistent weather, causing microbial contamination, nutrient degradation, and poor-quality products that limit market access and farmer incomes. Firewood drying also contributes to environmental harm due to CO2 emissions. Synnefa's Smart Solar Dryers use solar-powered HVAC systems and IoT sensors to improve post-harvest preservation. They precisely regulate temperature and humidity, preserving nutritional value and preventing microbial contamination. By implementing a Rent-to-Dry model this solution ensures affordable technology access for smallholder farmers through shared responsibility. Farmers can make usage-based payments for the drying services enabling access even for resource-constrained farmers. FarmCloud, the system's digital backbone, connects to dryers, providing real-time data on drying efficiency, environmental conditions, and production volumes. This enhances operational efficiency, compliance with quality standards, and access to high-value markets through traceability and transparency. The technology targets smallholder women and youth farmers in cooperatives and farmer groups, to reduce post-harvest losses, increase incomes, maintain food nutrition, encourage value addition, and contribute to a more sustainable food system by lowering carbon emissions. Through precise drying and value addition, farmers can access premium markets, improve their economic stability, and provide consumers with safer, more nutritious food products.

Project Title: PROMOTION OF  GRAIN AMARANTHUS CULTIVATION (A.cruentus) AND COMPOSITE FLOUR PRODUCTION FOR SUSTAINABLE NUTRITION AND ECONOMIC EMPOWERMENT IN TANZANIA
Executive Summary: Potential of grain amaranth in meeting  nutrition  needs makes our project  promotes  its cultivation to smallholder farmers , focusing on producing nutrient-rich composite flour using grain amaranths for local consumption. Formulating, scaling, grain amaranths food products and environmentally friendly processing methods, will improve food security, create economic opportunities to women, youth, SMEs, provide affordable, nutritious food. The initiative also promotes climate resilience, offering scalable solution to address malnutrition and support sustainable agricultural development.
Innovation Description: This project seeks to develop a nutritious composite flour (NCF) for a healthy diet based on underutilized amaranth grains, maize, and millet as an alternative to traditional diets. The innovative NCF will avert the problem of malnutrition and food insecurity, which is the effect of global food system challenges. The NCF will be formulated using linear programming at a specified ratio to provide 50-70% of Recommended Daily Allowances (RDA) of iron and zinc, safety and sensory done to ensure trust for consumers. By integrating the innovative composite flour into local diets, fosters a contribution initiative to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of zero hunger and no poverty by 2030. An education will be provided to raise awareness on the versatility and ease of cultivating amaranths for the sustainable production of innovative NCF while improving planetary health. Women and youth farmers will be supported to cultivate grain amaranths, encouraged to enter contract farming agreements with small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in food processing. SMEs will purchase amaranth grains from farmers, creating a reliable market for the crop and providing economic opportunities for local farmers. Amaranth roots, stems, and leaves will be used for poultry feed, poultry rewarding manures to grain amaranths. The model warrants NCF sustainable production, affordability, and equitable access by marginalized communities. Advocating decision-makers to integrate grain amaranths into food systems and public health programs. Solving these problems is critical because malnutrition not only causes needless human suffering but also reduces physical work productivity, learning capacity, and innovation

Long-term, the initiative enhances food security, boosts livelihoods, and establishes scalable models for sustainable agriculture. Project Title: Sustainable Poultry Production through Innovative Integrated Feed Solutions
Executive Summary: Tac-Maz Sustainable Ventures aims to enhance the supply of indigenous and dual-purpose chicken meat in Malawi by supporting smallholder farmers, particularly women, through contract farming. The project will provide start-up chicks, training on low-cost, climate-friendly supplementary feed, and improved poultry management. Tac-Maz will buy back the grown chickens, ensuring a consistent supply for the market. This 24-month initiative will strengthen the poultry supply chain, raise incomes for smallholders, and promote sustainable, resilient farming practices.
Innovation Description: The innovation aims to enhance the productivity and marketability of indigenous and dual-purpose chicken breeds in Malawi through a contract farming model that links smallholder farmers with Tac-Maz poultry farm. The problem being solved is the low productivity of these chickens, driven by fragmented production systems, poor feeding, and lack of quality breeding services. This is crucial due to the rising demand for indigenous chicken meat, which is valued for its health benefits and climate resilience.  The solution involves providing smallholder farmers with start-up chicks, training on low-cost, nutritious, and climate-friendly supplementary feeds, including the production of Black Soldier Flies (BSF), and offering an input-supply and buy-back arrangement. The BSF larvae are produced locally, reducing feed costs and contributing to environmentally sustainable practices. These larvae are rich in protein and make an excellent feed supplement, boosting chicken health and growth. Tac-Maz also utilizes alternative feeds, like moringa, pawpaw leaves, and maize bran.  Immediate benefits include higher farmer incomes, improved chicken quality and productivity, and cost savings from affordable, locally-produced feeds. The long-term benefits encompass improved food security, climate resilience for farmers, and reduced dependence on costly commercial feed. The innovation also supports women s economic empowerment, as 75% of the farmers are women. By strengthening the local poultry value chain and fostering sustainable practices, this solution benefits farmers, the environment, and society at large.

Executive Summary: Evidence-Based Research Council for Children s Health (EBRCCH): conduct an extensive review of existing academic research presenting an evidence-based meta-analysis of what types of foods, and diets more broadly, can be effective in creating healthy and thriving children. Innovation Description: The core problem is that low-income families spend most of their household income on food, and yet, 735 million people are malnourished. Our current food system structure prioritizes large-scale production, global connectivity, and the concentration of industry stakeholders. Animal-sourced foods are expensive and out-of-reach for low-income families but are seen as aspirational purchases, especially as household incomes increase. Current food system transformation programs include social behavior change campaigns that explain to low-income families why animal sourced foods are nutritionally important, resulting in low-income families spending large proportions of their household expenditure on small portions of expensive animal sourced foods that most often get consumed by the men of the household, and not by female household members or children. To address these problems Tailored Food will:   Evidence Based Council   Create an EAT-Lancet style research report, that will exist as a resource for all food system stakeholders and community-based advocacy groups, widely recognized as the evidence-based data needed to prove that children do grow to be healthy and thriving adults on a diverse range of plant-rich diets in different cultural and economic contexts around the world.   Multi-year Entrepreneur Partnerships   Scale bottom-up impact, collaborating with small-scale entrepreneurs in the countries most impacted by malnutrition, we launch and scale nutritious low-cost food products, with over 7.3 million meals produced and sold to date.   Strategic Consulting Projects for Larger Organizations  Scale top down impact, we complete food systems mapping, investment cases and strategic partnership building for clients such as UNICEF.

Project Title: Upcycling whey into biofertilizer and livestock feed using black soldier fly larvae (Hermetia illucens)
Executive Summary: This project proposes the development of an innovative system to collect and upcycle whey from cheese production by integrating a logistics optimization system and Black Soldier Fly Larvae (Hermetia illucens). This project will result in: 1) an efficient collection system for whey from small rural dairy facilities, 2) conversion of this byproduct into nutrient-rich biomass, ideal for supplement for livestock feed and 3) transformation of fermentation residues into organic fertilizer (high nitrogen content).
Innovation Description: Whey, a byproduct of the cheese industry, poses a significant environmental challenge if not properly managed, leading to soil and water contamination due to its elevated biological oxygen demand (BOD) and chemical oxygen demand (COD), which converts whey into a major pollutant worldwide. Globally, the cheese industry produces approximately 115 million tons of whey annually, with nearly 47% being discharged untreated into wastewater systems.  In rural communities and in small dairy facilities in Mexico, this issue is further exacerbated as whey is often discarded without treatment, intensifying pollution problems while overlooking its potential as a valuable resource. Additionally, whey production is highly dispersed, making its efficient collection and transportation a logistical challenge. Addressing these issues provides a critical opportunity to transform whey from an environmental liability into a key component of sustainable and circular economy solutions.  This proposal employs black soldier fly larvae (Hermetia illucens) to transform whey into nutrient-rich biomass and organic fertilizers. This biotechnological process leverages the larvae's ability to metabolize organic matter and convert it into high-quality proteins and lipids, ideal for livestock feed. Additionally, the residual material from larval cultivation is rich in nitrogen compounds, making it suitable for sustainable agriculture as fertilizer.  Immediate and long-term benefits: 1) Reduction of environmental pollution in rural communities, particularly by reducing waste disposal  problems from small-scale cheese producers; 2) Generation of sustainable, low-cost products for farmers and livestock producers; 3) Strengthening of economic development of rural communities.

Project Title: Demonstrating Impact for Growth: Charlie Cart s Evaluation of Hands-on Mobile Food Education
Executive Summary: The Charlie Cart Project  (CCP) Evaluation of Hands-on Mobile Food Education will analyze the impact of CCP programming on children participating in CCP lessons. We seek to understand our effectiveness in changing kids  attitudes and behaviors towards healthy food and in making food choices supportive of their health and of the environment. Understanding our impact on participants will enable us to bring hands-on food education to scale and help transform the food system.
Innovation Description: Food and cooking education is recognized as an effective prevention measure for children at risk of diet-related disease. Yet, most children receive just 8 hours annually, far below the 40 hours needed to make healthy, informed choices. Complicating this issue, most existing food education programs lack affordable, sustainable strategies to address the practical barriers to hands-on cooking instruction. At The Charlie Cart Project (CCP), we believe that if we can t bring kids to the kitchen, we can bring the kitchen to the kids.  CCP provides an innovative and accessible food education program, improving culinary literacy and nutritional access for communities nationwide. Our compact, mobile kitchen-on-wheels includes all the tools and equipment needed to get 30 participants cooking. Our program also includes training and resources for educators, and a 54-lesson K-5 standards-aligned curriculum. Our skills-focused curriculum is designed to expose students to a variety of new flavors and ingredients, while building their ability and confidence to prepare healthy meals from scratch.   Currently in 600+ communities in 47 states, CCP reaches 500,000 children each year with foundational skills to lead healthy, thriving lives. In a recent evaluation, over half the students tried a new food; the number of students who  loved  a food after a CCP class increased by 25%; 69% of participants want to make the recipe again. With support from IFT, CCP will fully measure impact on educators and participants, provide the evidence-base for exponential growth, and bring hands-on food education to scale across the country.
